title: How did Ben Matson die?
article: Two years after the truck driver lost his life during a violent police arrest, his grieving daughter still isn't sure where the truth lies
Julie Matson will never enjoy the storybook, father-and-daughter relationship she yearned to have with her Dad.
Her chance ended two years ago when Ben Matson, 49, died on a downtown sidewalk during a violent arrest by Vancouver police in the early hours of May 12, 2002.
Ben, who was a truck driver, had some demons to conquer, Julie recalls. A few years before his death, Ben checked himself into a treatment centre and licked a drug habit, or so Julie thought.
Father and daughter grew closer after that. They talked more and related better, says Julie, her eyes welling with tears.
Then, suddenly, he was gone. "He never saw me marry."
Regret over what might have been is partly behind Julie's push to find out what happened to her father the morning he died.
"I've already waited two years for this to be resolved. It's ridiculous -- nothing is happening."
She filed a complaint with B.C.'s police complaint commissioner but no ruling has yet been made. A coroner's inquest, mandatory in cases of police in-custody deaths, has yet to be scheduled.
What Julie and her lawyer, Rick Brooks, have been able to find out about Ben's death is confusing.
The autopsy report states he died from choking on his own vomit "due to or as a consequence of law enforcement restraint."

It also revealed cocaine in his blood and suggested drug use may have been a factor in his death. At .03 milligrams per litre, the level was not high enough to cause a lethal overdose. But it was within the range found in cocaine users who enter a state of what medical experts refer to as "excited delirium."
People in this agitated, violent state are reported to have superhuman strength and almost no reaction to pain, says Dr. James Cairns, Ontario's deputy chief coroner.
"We've had them where 12, 15 police officers can not restrain the guy . . . they're in overdrive."
Suspects in this state, seen more often now with the rise in popularity of cocaine and methamphetamine, are also more likely to die during an arrest.
Usually, their racing hearts just give out, said Cairns, who co- authored a study which analyzed 20 such deaths in Ontario.

"The most striking finding . . . was that all of those who died unexpectedly during or after an episode of excited delirium had been physically restrained," stated the study published in the June 1998 Canadian Medical Association Journal.
While the excited delirium death phenomenon is now recognized by police and health officials, the question of who is responsible is hugely controversial.

Some say the suspects are to blame because they took the drugs in the first place. Others argue police and health professionals must learn to recognize the signs and pull back on the force used during arrests.
Michael Conner, an Oregon psychologist and crisis intervention trainer, wrote about the issue in a paper last year.
Conner said it is almost impossible to tell the difference between somebody who has excited delirium and somebody who is "completely out of their minds on drugs and/or mentally ill and dangerous."
"You can't ask a police officer to be a physician and at the same time ask him to put his life at risk."
So what was going on with Ben Matson on the morning of his arrest?
Police believe cocaine drove him into a state of excited delirium. However, Julie's lawyer does not buy it.
"People who die from excited delirium don't die from choking to death. They die of heart failure," said Brooks. The autopsy report states clearly, police restraint caused Ben's death, he said.
He believes investigators spotted the cocaine reference in the autopsy and seized upon cocaine delirium as a defence for an overly aggressive arrest.

Initial media reports said Ben was in the Yale Hotel pub when he saw a man trying to move his Harley Davidson. Ben went out and argued with the man, an off-duty RCMP officer who was upset over where the bike was parked.

Ben Matson was no angel. But he was not a bike gang member and according to police had only a minor criminal record. But Julie wonders if her father's symbolic Harley Davidson raised undue suspicions in the minds of the police.
One of the off-duty Mounties thought he had seen something in Ben's hand during the argument and said so when he called the Vancouver police.
The call came in as a "man with a knife."
The police who responded were told at the door that the caller was mistaken -- that Ben was not carrying a knife -- but the adrenaline levels probably rem-ained high, Brooks says.
What happened next can not be explained by anyone, including the friends who were with Ben that night.
When police walked toward him, knifeless Ben raced out the back door.
The officers caught up with him in front of the Two Parrots restaurant. Witnesses present different accounts of what happened next.
Some say Ben was beaten relentlessly by police indifferent to his cries for mercy. Others say he fought like a cornered cougar and it was all police could do to subdue him.

One witness stated the arrest took a long time because "he \[Matson\] was going crazy, kicking." According to the autopsy, the police kicked, too. The report detailed six to eight blows to Ben's head, leaving patterns "consistent with footwear treads."
However, it found the blows were not serious enough to cause significant injury.
Vancouver Police Const. Sarah Bloor said the internal investigation is complete and found no fault with the arresting officers.
Matson's death was caused by his cocaine use, she said.

She said officers are trained to deal with cocaine psychosis, excited delirium and the danger of positional asphyxiation (suffocation while under restraint). The Vancouver police are examining new research and programs in the United States to see if anything can be added to the existing training in these areas, she said.
Julie hopes the coroner's inquest will provide more answers.
"It's heartbreaking talking to my grandma," she says. "She's almost 89 and doesn't have a lot to do. She just sits and dwells on it."

Julie still grieves, too. "It's hard because my dad, he's gone down some wrong roads in the past. But in the last few years of his life he was trying his hardest. He realized his mistakes and was trying to rectify them, make things better."
